articles.title: The dreamer who wants the world to read Nepali literature
articles.summary: Rishi Ram Adhikari, founder of Kitab Yatra and Kitab Jatra Festival, discusses his mission to promote Nepali literature globally, build libraries and connect readers across borders through cultural exchange.
articles.content:
The Kitab Jatra Festival has quickly become one of the most vibrant platforms for celebrating Nepali literature, books and culture. The Festival is organised and hosted by the Kitab Yatra Foundation, a Nepal-based organisation promoting literature, reading, art and cultural exchange. Since its launch in 2018, the festival has grown from a local gathering into a dynamic international event, connecting readers and writers not only across Nepal but also in India, the UK, and the USA, with plans to expand to Dubai, Australia, Portugal, Belgium and Germany. Working in collaboration with various organisations and institutions, it has created a global stage where Nepali voices are shared, celebrated and amplified.

At the heart of this movement is Rishi Ram Adhikari, Founder and Chairman of the Kitab Yatra Foundation and the Kitab Yatra book distribution company. In his early 30s, he emerged as a cultural entrepreneur dedicated to promoting Nepali literature and fostering a reading culture. His initiatives have not only expanded literary festivals abroad but also established over 20 libraries across Nepal and introduced scholarship programs for students.

Recognising these remarkable contributions, Kitab Yatra and Rishi Ram were honoured with the 5th edition of the Tally MSME Honours 2025 and the Public Choice ICT Award in 2019 for their pioneering efforts in enriching the Nepali literary world. This accolade further highlights his role as one of the leading advocates for Nepali literature today.

Sangita Swechcha from Global Voices interviewed Adhikari via email.

Sangita Swechcha (SS): What inspired you to start the Kitab Yatra book distribution company and the Kitab Jatra Festival at such a young age?

Rishi Ram Adhikari (RRA): My inspiration came from a simple but important realisation: books can transform individuals, and individuals can transform society. However, for that transformation to happen, books must be accessible, reading must become a habit and literature must be connected to people’s everyday lives.

Through Kitab Yatra, we began working to make books more accessible to readers across Nepal. But I gradually realised that distributing books alone was not enough. We also needed to create excitement around reading, bring writers and readers together, and make literature a part of public conversation. That realisation led to the Kitab Jatra Festival.

In my childhood, I listened to the chanting of my father reciting some slogans [from the epics] Mahabharat and Ramayan. While studying as a Chartered Accountant (CA) in New Delhi, India, despite my accounting career, I realised the value of words rather than numbers, so I dropped CA and came back to Nepal with four sacks of books and started an online bookstore in Kathmandu, Nepal. I believe young people should not wait for opportunities to create meaningful change; they should take the initiative to build them. Our journey has been driven by that belief, along with the dedication of our team, authors, partners and readers.

SS: How has the festival evolved since its beginnings in Nepal in 2018 to now being hosted in countries like the UK, USA, India, Portugal, Belgium, and Germany?

RRA: Since its beginning in 2018, Kitab Jatra has grown from a relatively small literary gathering into a broader platform for literature, culture and meaningful dialogue. What began with a limited number of voices and a single stage has developed into a festival bringing together writers, artists, thinkers, policymakers, entrepreneurs and readers from different generations.

The most important evolution has been in our ambition. We no longer see Nepali literature as something confined by geographical boundaries. Our international journey, including our work and outreach connected with the UK and other European countries, is an effort to connect Nepali writers with the diaspora and wider literary communities.

However, international expansion is not simply about taking a festival to another country. It is about building meaningful local partnerships, understanding the audience and creating a sustainable platform. Our goal is to make Kitab Jatra a bridge between Nepal and the world while ensuring that Nepali language, literature and cultural identity remain at its heart.

SS: What challenges do you face in promoting Nepali literature internationally, and how do you overcome them?

RRA: One of the biggest challenges is the limited international visibility of Nepali literature. We have talented writers, powerful stories, rich literary traditions and diverse cultural experiences, but many of these works remain inaccessible to international readers because of language barriers, limited translation opportunities, distribution challenges and insufficient global promotion.

Another challenge is sustainability. Organizing a meaningful literary festival requires financial resources, institutional partnerships, professional coordination and long-term commitment.

We are addressing these challenges by building partnerships with literary organizations, publishers, universities, diaspora institutions and cultural communities. We also want to encourage translation, book exchanges and conversations that introduce Nepali writing to audiences unfamiliar with our language and culture.

I believe we must move beyond simply asking the world to notice Nepali literature. We must create professional platforms, produce quality literary experiences and build lasting relationships that make such recognition possible. Our approach is to turn individual opportunities into long-term cultural connections.

SS: How do you see the role of the diaspora community in keeping Nepali literature and reading culture alive abroad?

RRA: The Nepali diaspora has a vital role in preserving and promoting our language, literature and cultural identity. For Nepalese living abroad, books can become a connection to their roots, history, memories, and sense of belonging. For younger generations growing up outside Nepal, literature can help them understand their heritage while encouraging them to explore their identity in a changing world.

I see the diaspora not merely as an audience but as an active partner in this literary journey. They can support Nepali authors, establish reading communities, organize literary discussions, introduce Nepali books to local libraries and connect our writers with international institutions.

Through Kitab Jatra’s international initiatives, we want to create spaces where these stories can travel across borders and where the diaspora can contribute to a living, evolving Nepali literary culture.

SS: Kitab Yatra Foundation has also been active inside Nepal, establishing libraries and supporting students — how do you balance its work at home and abroad?

RRA: For us, the work inside Nepal and our international initiatives are two sides of the same mission. We cannot talk about taking Nepali literature to the world while ignoring the need to make books accessible to people in our own communities.

Through our work in book distribution, library initiatives and student support, we aim to bring books closer to people — particularly those who have fewer opportunities to access them. Establishing libraries is not just about providing shelves and books; it is about creating spaces where curiosity can grow, young people can discover their potential, and communities can develop a lasting relationship with reading.

Internationally, we work to create visibility and opportunities for Nepali literature. At home, we work to strengthen the foundation from which that literature emerges. Balancing these responsibilities requires teamwork, partnerships and a clear sense of purpose.

Ultimately, success is not measured only by the size of a festival or the number of countries we reach. It is also measured by the child who discovers a love of reading, the student who receives an opportunity and the community that gains access to a library.

articles.personality_title: Bringing Nepali literature to the world through books and festivals
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Nepali literature has rich stories and traditions but is not well known outside Nepal. A young entrepreneur, Rishi Ram Adhikari, saw the need to share these stories globally and encourage people to read more in Nepal.

**What happened** – Since 2018, Adhikari has led the Kitab Jatra Festival, which started as a local event in Nepal and now takes place in countries like the UK, USA, India, Portugal, Belgium, and Germany. He also founded the Kitab Yatra Foundation to promote reading, build libraries across Nepal, and offer scholarships to students. His work has connected Nepali writers, readers, and the diaspora worldwide.

**Impact** – This effort helps Nepali literature reach new audiences despite language and distribution challenges. It also supports young readers and communities in Nepal by creating libraries and opportunities. The festival builds friendships between cultures and keeps Nepali heritage alive for people living abroad.

**What's next step** – Kitab Jatra plans to grow further into new countries like Dubai, Australia, and Germany. They aim to build stronger local partnerships, encourage book translations, and create lasting cultural connections that go beyond just events.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Rishi Ram Adhikari’s work is opening doors for Nepali literature worldwide while nurturing reading and culture at home through festivals, libraries, and scholarships.
articles.personality_title_fr: Faire connaître la littérature népalaise dans le monde grâce aux livres et aux festivals
articles.personality_presentation_fr:

**Ce qui s'est passé** – Depuis 2018, Adhikari dirige le Festival Kitab Jatra, qui a commencé comme un événement local au Népal et se déroule maintenant dans des pays comme le Royaume-Uni, les États-Unis, l’Inde, le Portugal, la Belgique et l’Allemagne. Il a aussi fondé la Fondation Kitab Yatra pour promouvoir la lecture, construire des bibliothèques au Népal et offrir des bourses aux étudiants. Son travail connecte les écrivains, lecteurs et la diaspora népalaise dans le monde entier.

**Impact** – Cette initiative permet à la littérature népalaise d’atteindre de nouveaux publics malgré les barrières linguistiques et de distribution. Elle soutient aussi les jeunes lecteurs et les communautés au Népal en créant des bibliothèques et des opportunités. Le festival crée des liens entre les cultures et maintient vivante l’héritage népalais pour ceux qui vivent à l’étranger.

**En résumé** – Le travail de Rishi Ram Adhikari ouvre des portes à la littérature népalaise dans le monde tout en nourrissant la lecture et la culture au Népal grâce aux festivals, bibliothèques et bourses.

articles.title: Daily briefing: Ancient cave art found hiding in plain sight
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 06 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03648-1Rock-art in a Spanish cave dates back 26,000 years. Plus, flexible working policies can end up saddling academic mothers with more work and the origins of Celtic and Germanic languages.
articles.content:
Rock-art in a Spanish cave dates back 26,000 years. Plus, flexible working policies can end up saddling academic mothers with more work and the origins of Celtic and Germanic languages.

Hello Nature readers, would you like to get this Briefing in your inbox free every day? Sign up here.

Inscriptions at the Cova de la Font Major cave system in Catalonia in northeastern Spain prompts rethink of prehistoric population and cultural trends. Credit: Vergès Bosch, J. M., Salas-Altès, M./Antiquity

Archaeologists have described hundreds of rock-art engravings dating back more than 25,000 years in a cave frequently visited by tourists in Catalonia — a region of northeastern Spain that was thought to be almost devoid of palaeolithic art. The cave system has been open to the public for decades and became a museum in the 1990s, but these motifs were missed because they “are really difficult to see”, says archaeologist and study co-author Míriam Salas-Altès. “You have to play with light from different directions to see the depressions.”

Nature | 4 min read

Reference: Antiquity paper

9.7 picokelvins The temperature to which scientists have cooled a cloud of rubidium atoms in an experiment on China’s Tiangong space station — the coldest ever attained experimentally. (Science | 5 min read) Reference: Science paper

Flexible working policies in academia, intended to make life easier, are having the opposite impact for many women. A survey of more than 10,000 academics with children found that women were more likely to do most of the parenting. That was partly because women used flexible hours to take on more caring responsibilities, whereas men in academic couples relied on their female partner to do the flexing.

Nature | 8 min read

Reference: Gender, Work & Organization paper & European Journal of Higher Education paper

NASA’s Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory, which gathered valuable data on cosmic explosions, has been destroyed by a fiery fall into Earth’s atmosphere. In August, NASA partnered with a private company to attempt a first-of-its-kind rescue mission to boost Swift back into orbit, but the LINK spacecraft wasn’t able to grab on.

CNN | 6 min read

Features & opinion

A farmer receives an unsatisfying answer to a burning question in The oracle of the second quadrant.

Nature | 6 min read

Andrew Robinson’s pick of five science books to read this week includes an exquisitely illustrated survey of plants with medical properties, an engrossing history of smell and an argument for the reality of time’s arrow.

Nature | 4 min read

Linguists and historians have long debated the origin stories of the Celtic and Germanic languages. To help shed light on where they might have come from, a team has looked at ancient DNA to trace the migration patterns of people who might have carried these languages with them as they moved across Europe.

Nature Podcast | 25 min listen

It has broad cultural and historical significance for the general public and provides substantial context about the discovery and its implications.
articles.personality_title: Ancient cave art found in Spain changes view of prehistoric culture
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – In northeastern Spain, the Catalonia region has many caves open to the public, but it was thought to have very little ancient rock art from the Paleolithic period, which is the time when early humans lived tens of thousands of years ago.

**What happened** – Archaeologists discovered hundreds of rock engravings inside the Cova de la Font Major cave that are over 25,000 years old. These artworks were missed for years because they are hard to see and only become clear when light hits them from certain angles. The cave has been a museum since the 1990s and is often visited by tourists.

**Impact** – This discovery shows that prehistoric people in this area created more art than previously believed. It changes how scientists understand the culture and movements of ancient populations in Europe. Finding such old art in a well-known cave surprises researchers and adds new details about human history.

**What's next step** – Researchers will study the designs more closely to learn what they might mean and how they relate to other ancient art in Europe. This could lead to new ideas about how early humans communicated and lived.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Ancient rock art over 25,000 years old found in a Spanish cave reveals more about prehistoric people and their culture than previously known.
articles.personality_title_fr: Une ancienne peinture rupestre découverte en Espagne change la vision de la culture préhistorique
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Dans la région de Catalogne, au nord-est de l’Espagne, de nombreuses grottes sont ouvertes au public, mais on pensait qu’il y avait très peu d’art rupestre ancien datant de la période paléolithique, époque où vivaient les premiers humains il y a des dizaines de milliers d’années.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Des archéologues ont découvert des centaines de gravures rupestres dans la grotte Cova de la Font Major, datant de plus de 25 000 ans. Ces œuvres d’art étaient passées inaperçues pendant des années car elles sont difficiles à voir et ne deviennent visibles que sous certains angles de lumière. La grotte est un musée depuis les années 1990 et est souvent visitée par des touristes.

**Impact** – Cette découverte montre que les habitants préhistoriques de cette région ont créé plus d’art qu’on ne le pensait auparavant. Elle modifie la compréhension scientifique des cultures et des déplacements des populations anciennes en Europe. Trouver un art aussi ancien dans une grotte connue surprend les chercheurs et apporte de nouveaux détails sur l’histoire humaine.

**Prochaines étapes** – Les chercheurs vont étudier plus en détail ces dessins pour comprendre leur signification et leur lien avec d’autres arts anciens en Europe. Cela pourrait conduire à de nouvelles idées sur la façon dont les premiers humains communiquaient et vivaient.

**Résumé en une phrase** – Une peinture rupestre vieille de plus de 25 000 ans découverte dans une grotte espagnole révèle davantage sur les peuples préhistoriques et leur culture qu’on ne le savait auparavant.
articles.personality_title_es: Arte rupestre antiguo encontrado en España cambia la visión de la cultura prehistórica
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – En la región de Cataluña, en el noreste de España, hay muchas cuevas abiertas al público, pero se creía que tenían muy poco arte rupestre antiguo del período paleolítico, cuando vivían los primeros humanos hace decenas de miles de años.

**Qué pasó** – Arqueólogos descubrieron cientos de grabados en la cueva Cova de la Font Major que tienen más de 25,000 años. Estas obras de arte pasaron desapercibidas durante años porque son difíciles de ver y solo se hacen visibles cuando la luz las ilumina desde ciertos ángulos. La cueva es un museo desde la década de 1990 y la visitan muchos turistas.

**Impacto** – Este descubrimiento muestra que las personas prehistóricas en esta zona hicieron más arte del que se pensaba. Cambia la forma en que los científicos entienden la cultura y los movimientos de las poblaciones antiguas en Europa. Encontrar arte tan antiguo en una cueva conocida sorprende a los investigadores y aporta nuevos detalles sobre la historia humana.

**Próximo paso** – Los investigadores estudiarán los diseños con más detalle para aprender qué podrían significar y cómo se relacionan con otros artes antiguos en Europa. Esto podría llevar a nuevas ideas sobre cómo se comunicaban y vivían los primeros humanos.

**Conclusión en una frase** – El arte rupestre de más de 25,000 años encontrado en una cueva española revela más sobre los pueblos prehistóricos y su cultura de lo que se conocía antes.
